sources.name: The New York Times - Glowing Auras and Black Money

desc: New York is where the modern disclosure movement acquired institutional legitimacy, on a single date. On 16 December 2017 The New York Times published 'Glowing Auras and Black Money: The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program' by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal and Leslie Kean, revealing the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, its roughly $22 million in funding, Luis Elizondo's resignation letter, and two of the Navy infrared videos. That story did not add a single new physical fact about any object; what it added was a masthead. Every subsequent institutional step - the Navy's 2019 designation of the objects as UAP, the 2020 Department of Defense release, the UAP Task Force, the ODNI assessment, the hearings, AARO - runs downstream of the decision made in a New York newsroom to treat the subject as a defence-accountability story rather than a curiosity. Blumenthal and Kean later moved much of their work to The Debrief, where on 5 June 2023 they published David Grusch's allegations after other outlets declined; Ross Coulthart's NewsNation reporting is produced from New York; The Intercept's Ken Klippenstein and Keith Kloor have run the sceptical counter-line from the same city. New York is therefore both the venue of the disclosure movement's decisive act and the venue of its most sustained internal argument about evidentiary standards.
